chunks: Ali, from his father, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from al-Minqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a city from the cities of the people of war: is it permissible to direct water against them and to burn it with fire, or to bombard it with catapults until they are killed, when among them are women, children, the aged elderly, Muslim captives, and merchants?
He (AS) said: 'One may do that to them, and one should not hold back from them because of these (people). And there is no blood money (diya) upon them for the Muslims, nor any expiation (kaffara).'

And I asked him about women — how the jizyah has fallen from them and been lifted from them. He (AS) said: 'Because the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) forbade fighting against women and children in the abode of war, except if they fight. If she (a woman) fights as well, then hold back from her as much as you can while not fearing a breach (in the battle line).'

Since he forbade killing them in the abode of war, then in the abode of Islam it is all the more so. And if she refused to pay the jizyah, killing her would not be possible. Since killing her is not possible, the jizyah is therefore lifted from her.

And if men refused to pay the jizyah, they would be violators of the covenant, and their blood would be licit and their killing (permissible) — because killing men is permissible in the land of polytheism. Similarly, the crippled among the people of dhimmah, the blind, the dying elderly, the woman, and children in the land of war — for this reason the jizyah is lifted from them.

key_terms.أَهْل الذِّمَّة: ahl al-dhimma (dhimmis) — non-Muslim subjects living under Muslim governance who pay jizyah and receive protection
key_terms.الْجِزْيَة: jizyah — the poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects (dhimmis) living under Muslim governance in exchange for protection
key_terms.الْمَجَانِيق: manjaniq (pl. majaniq) — a catapult or trebuchet, a medieval siege weapon
key_terms.دَار الْإِسْلَام: dar al-Islam — 'abode of Islam'; territories under Muslim governance where Islamic law is implemented
key_terms.دَار الْحَرْب: dar al-harb — 'abode of war'; territories not under Muslim governance, whose inhabitants are considered in a state of war with the Muslim community
key_terms.دِيَة: diya — blood money/wergild; monetary compensation paid to the family of a killed person in lieu of retaliation
key_terms.كَفَّارَة: kaffara — expiation/atonement; acts of worship performed to atone for certain sins or legal violations
key_terms.نَاقِضِين لِلْعَهْد: breakers of the covenant — those who violate the dhimma agreement, thereby forfeiting its protections

ai.seo_question: Does Islamic law permit using catapults and siege weapons against enemy cities when non-combatants are present, and why are women exempt from jizyah?
ai.summary: This hadith presents Imam al-Sadiq (AS) ruling on two related questions of Islamic military jurisprudence (jihad fiqh): first, that it is permissible to employ siege weapons (flooding, fire, catapults) against an enemy city even when vulnerable non-combatants are present, without incurring blood money or expiation; and second, explaining why women are exempt from jizyah (the poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects). The Imam derives the jizyah exemption for women from the Prophet's prohibition against killing women and children in war — since they cannot lawfully be killed if they refuse payment, the financial obligation itself cannot be enforced and is therefore removed. The hadith also specifies that this exemption extends to other categories who could not be killed — the physically disabled (al-muq'ad), the blind, the dying elderly — grouping them with women and children as non-combatants whose exemption flows from the same legal principle.
